story.text: Most failed rain gardens fail for one of four reasons, and all four are decided before a plant goes in the ground.
## The four

- **No overflow.** The single most common and most expensive failure. Water that cannot leave the garden goes toward the house.
- **Compacted bottom.** The excavator ran over the floor of the hole. Infiltration measured before excavation no longer describes the site after it.
- **Wrong soil mix.** Native clay backfilled because the sand mix cost money. The garden becomes a pond.
- **Sized off a guess.** Nobody measured the roof area actually draining to the downspout.
Every one of these is visible in the first heavy storm. Walk the garden during rain, not after.
Back to [[Rain Garden Guide]]; plant choices are in [[Rain Garden Plants]].

story.text: A rain garden is a shallow planted depression that takes roof and driveway runoff and lets it soak in instead of running to the storm drain. It is the cheapest piece of green stormwater infrastructure a household can build, and the one most likely to be built wrong.
## Why it works

Runoff from an impervious surface arrives fast, warm, and carrying whatever was on the pavement. A rain garden slows it, cools it, and hands it to soil biology and plant roots, which do the treatment. Nothing in it is exotic — the whole design is a hole, a soil mix, an overflow, and plants that tolerate both flood and drought.
The three numbers that decide whether it works:

- **Infiltration rate** — measured, not assumed. Dig a test hole, fill it, time the drop. Below half an inch per hour, build something else.
- **Sizing ratio** — garden area as a fraction of the impervious area draining to it. Five to ten percent is the usual band.
- **Ponding depth** — six to nine inches. Deeper looks efficient and drowns the plants.
See also [[Rain Garden Plants]] and [[Rain Garden Failures]].
## Build sequence
**Step:** Test — **What you do:** Percolation test at the actual location and depth — **What goes wrong:** Testing topsoil, then digging into clay
**Step:** Excavate — **What you do:** Flat bottom, not a bowl — **What goes wrong:** A bowl concentrates flow in the middle
**Step:** Amend — **What you do:** 60% sand, 30% compost, 10% topsoil — **What goes wrong:** Using native soil because it is free
**Step:** Inlet — **What you do:** Armor the entry with cobble — **What goes wrong:** Bare soil at the inlet erodes in one storm
**Step:** Overflow — **What you do:** Set the outlet at ponding depth — **What goes wrong:** No overflow, so the garden fails to the foundation
**Step:** Plant — **What you do:** Zones by tolerance, not by looks — **What goes wrong:** One species everywhere

story.text: Plant selection is a zoning problem, not a shopping problem. A rain garden has three moisture zones and a plant that thrives in one will sulk or die in another.
## The three zones

- **Bottom** — floods for hours after every storm, then dries hard. Sedges and rushes.
- **Slope** — wet feet occasionally, otherwise ordinary garden conditions. The widest choice.
- **Rim** — never floods. Treat it as normal planting bed; it is the part the neighbors see.
Density matters more than species. A sparsely planted rain garden is a weed nursery for its first two seasons, and the weeds win. Plant it thick the first year and thin it later.
Back to [[Rain Garden Guide]].
